comment: Reference stays for the IPPS payment parity run (ADR 024 step 5).
Every figure here is invented. There is no member, no claim number and no
real provider: the CMS certification numbers are fabricated and chosen only
so their first two digits are a plausible state code, because CMS's pricer
reads the state from them. The wage-index localities are real published CBSA
codes, which is public reference data and the only way to exercise the real
`why` says what each row pins. A row that pins nothing does not belong here:
the corpus is for distinguishing a correct calculator from a plausible wrong
`providerDefaults` holds the fields CMS's pricer requires before it will
price anything at all, with the values that mean 'none of this applies'.
Five of them are traps and are commented where they sit.

cases.name: wage-index-below-one
cases.why: 42 CFR 412.64(h)(3): below a wage index of 1.0 the statutory 62 percent labor share pays more, so it is the one CMS must use. Pins IppsRateSet.ShareFor on the low side.

cases.name: wage-index-above-one
cases.why: The other side of the same comparison: above 1.0 the annual rule's larger labor share pays more. A calculator that hard-codes one share fails exactly one of these two rows.

cases.name: alaska-cost-of-living
cases.why: 412.64(m)(1)(ii) lifts the non-labor share in Alaska. This is the row where the comparison and the 'wage index above 1.0' shortcut can disagree, and the one CHO's own test predicts the smaller labor share wins.

cases.name: teaching-hospital
cases.why: 412.105: the indirect medical education factor is ((1 + ratio) ^ 0.405 - 1) x 1.35. Pins IppsTeachingPolicy against CMS's own arithmetic rather than against my reading of it.

cases.name: disproportionate-share
cases.why: 412.106: the DSH adjustment, and 412.106(f)'s 75 percent reduction. CHO takes the adjustment factor as an input; CMS derives it from the SSI and Medicaid ratios, so this row is also the test of whether that difference matters to the paid amount.

cases.name: cost-outlier
cases.why: 412.84: charges far above the threshold, with both cost-to-charge ratios set. The row that catches the fixed-loss-amount double count, because a calculator testing operating and capital separately pays visibly more here.

cases.name: no-outlier-just-below-threshold
cases.why: The same hospital with charges chosen to sit under the threshold. An outlier calculation that is wrong in the generous direction pays something here, and nothing should be paid.

cases.name: transfer-per-diem-short-stay
cases.why: 412.4: review code 03 is the per-diem transfer. Length of stay 1 against DRG 871's geometric mean of 4.8 days, so two per diems are paid out of 4.8 and the payment is a fraction of the DRG.

cases.name: transfer-per-diem-capped-at-full
cases.why: 412.4 caps the per diem at the full DRG payment. Length of stay 9 against a geometric mean of 4.8 would otherwise pay more than a discharge, which is the error the cap exists to prevent.

cases.name: transfer-zero-length-of-stay
cases.why: A same-day transfer. CMS floors the length of stay at one day before adding the extra first-day per diem, so this stay is paid two per diems out of 4.8 and not one. CHO adds one to the length of stay as given, which pays one.

cases.name: transfer-fifty-fifty-special-payment-drg
cases.why: 412.4(f)(2)'s half-and-half transfer, review code 09. Which transfer rule a stay gets is a property of the DRG table — postAcuteCare and specialPaymentPostAcuteCare — and not something the caller asserts, which is where CHO's IppsStay flag puts it.

cases.name: burn-drg-outlier-marginal-cost
cases.why: 412.84(l) pays 90 percent of the excess rather than 80 for the burn DRGs. DRG 927 with charges well over the threshold, so the marginal cost factor is visible in the amount.

cases.name: long-stay-no-transfer
cases.why: A plain discharge well past the geometric mean. Nothing should be adjusted: the row that catches a calculator applying a per diem to ordinary discharges.

cases.name: quality-indicator-withheld
cases.why: A hospital that did not meet the quality reporting requirement. CMS pays it from a reduced standardized amount, which changes the labor and non-labor split itself. CHO's IppsRateSet holds one standardized amount and cannot express this.

cases.name: quality-indicator-withheld-above-one
cases.why: CMS table row 2: the quality reduction above a wage index of 1.0. With the row below it this says the two axes are independent -- the reduced hospital gets the 66 percent split of its own smaller amount, not the 62 percent split of anything.

cases.name: record-reduction-above-one
cases.why: CMS table row 5: the reduction for not being a meaningful electronic health record user, which is a smaller standardized amount again and independent of the quality requirement.

cases.name: record-reduction-and-quality-withheld-above-one
cases.why: CMS table row 6: both reductions at once. A hospital carrying both is paid a fourth published amount, not two reductions applied in turn, which is the whole reason CMS publishes eight rows rather than a reduction factor.

cases.name: record-reduction-below-one
cases.why: CMS table row 7: the record reduction at or below a wage index of 1.0.

cases.name: record-reduction-and-quality-withheld-below-one
cases.why: CMS table row 8: both reductions at or below 1.0. The eighth row, which completes the table the parity test builds and so is what lets the test assert CHO picked the same row CMS did rather than only that its arithmetic was self-consistent.

cases.name: readmissions-reduction
cases.why: 412.154's readmissions adjustment, which CMS takes as (factor - 1) times the base DRG payment and carries as a signed amount in the sum. The hospital also has an uncompensated care payment, so a calculator taking the adjustment on the whole operating side rather than on the base payment alone disagrees here.

cases.name: value-based-purchasing-bonus
cases.why: The value-based purchasing adjustment paying more rather than less. CMS's range is 0.98 to 2.0, where the readmissions range stops at 1.0, which is why the two cannot be one input.

cases.name: low-volume-adjustment
cases.why: 412.101's low-volume uplift on a cost outlier case, which is what pins its base: CMS takes it on both sides, the outlier and the uncompensated care payment, not on the DRG amount. A calculator taking it on the base payment is wrong by the most on exactly these cases.

cases.name: hospital-acquired-condition-penalty
cases.why: 412.170's one percent penalty on an outlier case. It is one percent of the assembled payment and not of the DRG amount, so on an outlier it is several times what a 'one percent reduction' reading would give.

cases.name: all-four-adjustments-in-order
cases.why: All four at once, on a cost outlier case with an uncompensated care payment. This is the row that pins the ORDER: the low-volume uplift is taken on everything through the outlier but not on the other two adjustments, and the penalty is one percent of all of it together. Any other ordering agrees on each adjustment in isolation and disagrees here.

cases.name: sole-community-own-rate-wins
cases.why: 42 CFR 412.92: a sole community hospital whose own rate beats the federal one is paid the difference. Pins the hospital-specific portion, and with it the update factor -- the one number that cannot be derived, because CMS restarted the cumulative prior-year chain at 1.0 for FY2026 after carrying every update back to FY2019 through FY2025.

cases.name: sole-community-federal-rate-wins
cases.why: The same hospital with a lower facility rate, so the federal side wins and the portion is zero. Pins the comparison as a comparison: an implementation that added the two together instead of taking the greater pays roughly double here and agrees on the row above.

cases.name: medicare-dependent-seventy-five-percent
cases.why: 42 CFR 412.108: a Medicare-dependent small rural hospital is paid 75 percent of the difference, not all of it. The only thing separating the three categories, and the row that catches paying it in full.

cases.name: essential-access-community-hospital
cases.why: Provider type 21. Paid on the sole community terms rather than the Medicare-dependent ones, which is worth pinning because the three categories are three disjoint pairs of provider type codes and getting a pair into the wrong branch costs 25 percent of the portion.

cases.name: sole-community-record-reduction
cases.why: A sole community hospital carrying the electronic health record reduction. The two payment-reduction flags cut the payment twice through two different numbers -- a smaller row of the rate table and a smaller hospital-specific update factor -- and a calculator that applied the flags to only one of them agrees with CMS on neither side.

cases.name: sole-community-transfer-full-weight
cases.why: A per-diem transfer at a sole community hospital. The federal side of the comparison carries the transfer fraction and the hospital-specific rate carries the FULL DRG weight, so a short transfer lands on the hospital-specific side almost whatever the facility rate is. That asymmetry is in CMS's program and not in the regulation, which is exactly why it needs a row.

cases.name: sole-community-outlier-and-adjustments
cases.why: A sole community hospital with a cost outlier on both sides, an uncompensated care payment, the low-volume adjustment and the hospital-acquired-condition penalty at once. The charges are tuned so that the portion survives: CMS pays 3,984.58 here without the outlier and 2,294.26 with it, which is the 1,690.32 operating outlier taken off dollar for dollar, while the 5,394.00 capital outlier does not touch it at all. That is the row that pins what is inside the comparison -- the operating outlier and the uncompensated care payment, and no part of the capital payment -- and then that the portion is inside both the low-volume base and the penalty base.
